questions.q: A 2-week-old girl presents with linear, punctate atrophic lesions on her trunk and limbs that follow a specific anatomical distribution. Investigation reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the PORCN gene on chromosome Xp11.23. Which of the following best explains why approximately 90% of Goltz Syndrome cases occur in females?
opts: Females have two copies of the X chromosome, providing a selective survival advantage over males
The PORCN mutation causes hemizygous lethality in non-mosaic males in utero, while females survive via functional mosaicism from X-inactivation
Males have stronger Wnt signaling pathway activation that protects against PORCN mutations
Females are preferentially exposed to environmental triggers that activate PORCN gene expression
questions.exp: Goltz Syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by PORCN mutations. Because the mutation is typically lethal in non-mosaic hemizygous males in utero, approximately 90% of affected patients are female. Females survive through random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization), creating functional mosaicism with both normal and defective cells.

questions.q: A dermatologist evaluates a 5-year-old with unilateral temporal alopecia. The child's mother asks if this could be due to a genetic mutation. Which statement most accurately reflects the genetic and inheritance pattern of triangular alopecia?
opts: It is an autosomal dominant condition with strong HLA-associated susceptibility
It is a mosaic developmental defect with paradominant inheritance and no specific HLA associations
It is exclusively an acquired condition triggered by trauma during hair growth
It is an X-linked recessive disorder with variable penetrance in females
questions.exp: Triangular alopecia is primarily a congenital mosaic disease with paradominant inheritance pattern. Because it is a developmental/structural defect rather than an autoimmune disorder, it completely lacks HLA associations and pathogenic autoantibodies.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A MOSAIC (mixed cellular) KING (paradominant) sits on the THRONE with NO FLAGS (no HLA)—this castle was built WRONG from the blueprints, not conquered by enemies.

questions.q: A newborn with Sturge-Weber syndrome has a capillary malformation involving the V1 (ophthalmic) and V2 (maxillary) distributions. At 6 weeks, the parents notice the infant has not yet developed seizures. Which embryological concept best explains why this infant has simultaneous facial PWS, leptomeningeal involvement, and risk of choroidal pathology?
opts: The GNAQ mutation arose during late neural-crest migration, after facial tissue differentiation was complete
The GNAQ mutation occurred very early in the anterior neural crest before widespread migration, allowing the mutant clone to populate the frontonasal prominence and its derivatives
Separate GNAQ mutations independently arose in skin, brain, and eye tissue during organogenesis
The leptomeningeal and choroidal malformations are secondary to progressive dilatation from the primary facial port-wine stain
questions.exp:
The key to understanding the SWS triad is that a single early GNAQ somatic mutation in the anterior neural crest before migration allows one mutant clone to populate all derivatives of the frontonasal prominence: the upper-facial cutaneous vasculature, the leptomeninges overlying cortex, and the ocular choroid. This single clonal origin explains the simultaneous and ipsilateral involvement.
🏰 Palace: Picture the NEURAL CREST as a ROYAL CASTLE FACTORY—the GNAQ mutation is stamped onto a SINGLE MASTER BLUEPRINT at the very START of production. That one defective blueprint is then photocopied and distributed to the FOREHEAD BUILDERS (facial PWS), BRAIN LINING WORKERS (leptomeninges), and EYE JEWEL SETTERS (choroid)—all receiving the same defect from ONE source.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a well-demarcated, irregularly bordered tan-brown patch on his left shoulder that has progressively darkened and now shows coarse terminal hair growth over it. The lesion has an archipelago-like appearance with jagged outlines. Which of the following genetic and molecular mechanisms BEST explains the pathophysiology of this lesion?
opts: Autosomal dominant mutations in KIT gene with loss of melanocyte function
Postzygotic somatic mutations in ACTB gene causing Hedgehog pathway potentiation and pilar smooth muscle dysfunction
HLA-associated autoimmune destruction of melanocytes in a segmental distribution
Germline mutations in PTEN gene leading to hamartomatous overgrowth
questions.exp:
Becker's nevus is driven by postzygotic somatic mutations in the ACTB gene (beta-actin) that potentiate Hedgehog pathway signaling and disrupt normal hair follicle and pilar muscle development, primarily affecting pilosebaceous units and arrector pili smooth muscles. Unlike autoimmune conditions, it lacks pathogenic antibodies, autoantigens, or HLA associations, and follows a paradominant (mostly sporadic) inheritance pattern.
🏰 Palace: Picture a young boy's SHOULDER with an ARCHIPELAGO of islands forming an A-shape, where ACTB (Actin-Beta) molecules are ACTING as tiny HEDGEHOG-shaped dancers in the pilar muscles, making them hyperplastic during puberty.

questions.q: An outbreak of hand-foot-and-mouth disease in Singapore has resulted in severe neurological complications including brainstem encephalitis and acute flaccid paralysis in multiple children under 5 years of age. Which enterovirus is responsible for this severe variant?
opts: Coxsackievirus A4
Coxsackievirus A6
Enterovirus 71
Echovirus 6
questions.exp: Enterovirus 71 (EV-A71) causes the severe/neurologic variant of HFMD with dangerous tropism for the central nervous system and cardiopulmonary tissues, leading to brainstem encephalitis, encephalomyelitis, and aseptic meningitis. This virus shows a striking geographic predilection for the Asia-Pacific region since the late 1990s, with children under 5 years experiencing the highest mortality risk.

questions.q: A 2-day-old female infant with restrictive dermopathy born following a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and decreased fetal movements dies from respiratory insufficiency. Which population has an exceptionally high carrier frequency for ZMPSTE24 mutations, estimated at 1 in 21?
opts: Ashkenazi Jewish populations in Israel
Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations in North America, particularly South Dakota
Sub-Saharan African populations with sickle cell trait
Japanese populations with hereditary ichthyosis
questions.exp: A specific shared founder mutation is highly prevalent in the Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations in North America, where carrier status is exceptionally high, estimated at up to 1 in 21 in Hutterite populations from South Dakota. This high frequency reflects founder effects and consanguinity within these closed communities.

questions.q: A 2-day-old full-term male infant presents with scattered erythematous macules and pustules on the cheeks, trunk, and buttocks. The mother is concerned about infection. Wright–Giemsa smear of pustular fluid shows predominantly eosinophils with no bacterial or fungal organisms. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this eruption?
opts: Transfer of maternal autoreactive lymphocytes triggering a graft-versus-host-like reaction
Localised innate-immune response to commensal microbes colonising hair follicles and triggering acute-phase inflammation
Primary bacterial infection from vaginal flora requiring immediate antibiotic therapy
Maternal IgE antibodies crossing the placenta and causing mast cell degranulation in neonatal skin
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN) is pathogenically explained by a localised innate-immune response to commensal skin bacteria that colonise and penetrate hair follicles shortly after birth. The historical graft-versus-host hypothesis has been disproven; lesions show no demonstrable maternal cells. The condition is sterile and self-limited, reflecting maturation of the neonatal immune system with elevated pro-inflammatory mediators (IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8) and perifollicular mast cell accumulation.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with a well-demarcated triangular patch of hair loss in the left temporal region. Dermoscopy shows fine vellus hairs replacing normal terminal hairs. Histology demonstrates no perifollicular inflammation. Which of the following best explains the pathomechanism of this condition?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of hair follicles with CD8+ T-cell infiltration
Localized miniaturization of terminal hairs with preserved follicle density and absence of inflammation
Developmental aplasia of hair follicles with reduced follicle count
Immunobullous disruption of the hair-follicle junction
questions.exp: Triangular alopecia is a non-inflammatory, non-scarring developmental defect characterized by normal follicle density but profound miniaturization where terminal hairs are replaced by fine vellus hairs. Histology explicitly shows absence of perifollicular or bulbar inflammation, distinguishing it from autoimmune conditions like alopecia areata.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a TEMPLE (temporal) filled with TINY GHOSTS (vellus hairs) still DANCING in normal numbers—the follicles aren't destroyed, just shrunk and DEFLATED into delicate wisps; no angry immune knights battering the walls.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with sharply demarcated, coin-shaped plaques measuring 2 cm in diameter on the extensor surfaces of the arms. The lesions are dull red, intensely pruritic, and show prominent weeping with heavy crust formation. Histology reveals intense intercellular edema with spongiosis primarily affecting which layers?
opts: Dermis and subcutaneous fat
Epidermis and upper dermis with reduced desmosomes in the basal layer
Stratum corneum and stratum granulosum exclusively
Deep dermis with intact basal layer desmosomes
questions.exp: Exudative nummular eczema shows primary pathology in the epidermis and upper superficial dermis. The key histological finding is intense intercellular edema (spongiosis) causing a reduction in desmosomes between basal layer cells, while desmosomes in the overlying stratum spinosum are largely preserved. This pattern distinguishes nummular eczema from other eczematous conditions.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a COIN-SHAPED moat (nummular) around the castle's BASE (basal layer), where the drawbridge chains (desmosomes) are BREAKING, but the upper STONE WALLS (stratum spinosum) remain SOLID—water seeps through only at the foundation.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with symmetric, pruritic papulovesicular lesions on the face, buttocks, and extensor surfaces of the extremities. Laboratory investigations reveal active EBV infection, but liver function tests are normal with no jaundice. Which of the following best describes this presentation?
opts: Classic Papular Acrodermatitis associated with Hepatitis B surface antigen
Papulovesicular Acrolocated Syndrome triggered by EBV, lacking hepatitis
Adult-onset variant of Gianotti-Crosti syndrome
Atypical presentation with palmar and plantar involvement
questions.exp: This clinical presentation—pruritic papulovesicular lesions without hepatitis in a young child with EBV infection—is characteristic of Papulovesicular Acrolocated Syndrome (non-HBV associated), which is now the most frequently encountered form since HBV vaccination became routine. The key distinguishing features of this form include lack of hepatitis, pronounced pruritus, vesicular morphology, and prolonged course, contrasting with classic HBV-associated disease.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man of Jewish ancestry presents with widespread, extremely pruritic discoid lesions that simultaneously display both exudative (weeping) and lichenoid (thickened, leathery) phases. Based on the epidemiological and clinical presentation, which variant of nummular eczema is most likely?
opts: Dry nummular dermatitis with minimal itching
Nummular dermatitis of the hands following occupational exposure
Exudative discoid and lichenoid chronic dermatosis (Sulzberger-Garbe syndrome)
Classic exudative nummular eczema in children
questions.exp: Exudative discoid and lichenoid chronic dermatosis (Sulzberger-Garbe syndrome or Oid-oid disease) is a distinctive variant occurring almost exclusively in adult males of Jewish ancestry aged 40–60 years, characterized by rapidly alternating or simultaneous exudative and lichenoid phases with intense pruritus. After a chronic, intractable course lasting months to years, it typically ends in spontaneous cure.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a JEWISH GENTLEMAN (40–60 years old) standing at a castle gate wearing a LEATHER JACKET (lichenoid) that's SOAKING WET (exudative) simultaneously—he FLIPS between the two states like a COIN, but eventually the curse BREAKS and he walks free.

questions.q: Histopathological examination of skin lesions in Gianotti-Crosti syndrome reveals epidermal spongiosis, mild acanthosis, parakeratosis, and a perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Which layers of the skin are characteristically affected in the classic HBV-associated form?
opts: Epidermis and subcutaneous fat
Epidermis and superficial dermis
Deep dermis and hypodermis
Dermis only, with intact epidermis
questions.exp: Classic Papular Acrodermatitis of Childhood (HBV-associated) characteristically affects the epidermis and superficial dermis, as demonstrated by histology showing epidermal spongiosis, acanthosis, parakeratosis, and patchy perivascular lymphocytic or lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrates in the dermis. This limited depth of involvement distinguishes it from deeper cutaneous conditions.

questions.q: A 3-day-old neonate presents with fever, irritability, and a rapidly spreading orange-red macular rash beginning on the face and spreading to intertriginous areas. Within 48 hours, large flaccid bullae develop, rupture to leave raw denuded areas, and characteristic radial fissuring appears around the mouth and nose. Intraoral mucosa remains completely intact. Which molecular mechanism explains the sparing of mucous membranes in this condition?
opts: Mucosal surfaces have higher Desmoglein-1 concentration, providing resistance to exfoliative toxins
Mucous membranes primarily rely on Desmoglein-3 for cellular adhesion, which is unaffected by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins
Salivary IgA antibodies neutralize exfoliative toxins before they can reach mucosal cells
The stratum granulosum is thicker in mucosal epithelium, preventing toxin-mediated cleavage
questions.exp:
Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA and ETB) specifically target and cleave Desmoglein-1, which is the primary adhesion molecule in superficial epidermis. Mucous membranes rely predominantly on Desmoglein-3 for cell-to-cell adhesion, which is structurally different and completely resistant to these toxins, resulting in absolute mucosal sparing despite widespread cutaneous involvement.
🏰 Palace: Imagine mucosal surfaces wearing DSG-3 ARMOR SHIELDS while the epidermis below wears DSG-1 PAPER ARMOR—only the paper tears when the staphylococcal SWORD (exfoliative toxin) swings through.

questions.q: A 3-month-old boy presents with a purple port-wine stain over the left forehead and upper eyelid. His parents ask if this is inherited. Genetic testing reveals a somatic GNAQ c.548G>A mutation in the lesional tissue only. What is the most accurate counselling regarding recurrence risk in future siblings?
opts: 25% recurrence risk; autosomal recessive inheritance
Virtually no recurrence risk; this is a postzygotic somatic mosaic mutation
50% recurrence risk; autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance
Recurrence risk depends on whether the mother is a germline carrier
questions.exp:
Sturge-Weber syndrome results from a postzygotic somatic GNAQ mutation occurring after fertilisation in a single neural-crest cell, affecting only that clone's descendants. Because the mutation is not present in the germline, there is no transmission to offspring and recurrence risk in siblings is virtually zero, unlike inherited neurocutaneous syndromes.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a CASTLE WALL being painted with a PURPLE WINE STAIN (SWS) by a SINGLE PAINTER who only painted THAT WALL—the paint never reached the BLUEPRINT HOUSE PLANS (germline), so future houses built from the original blueprint won't have that stain.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant with localized bullous impetigo in the axilla caused by Staphylococcus aureus is referred to dermatology. The mother asks why her child's infection remains limited to the skin fold rather than spreading systemically like her older brother who had generalized SSSS (Ritter's disease) as a neonate. Which factor is responsible for the localized versus generalized phenotype in staphylococcal exfoliative toxin disease?
opts: Infants with localized bullous impetigo possess neutralizing antibodies against exfoliative toxins that older neonates with SSSS lack
The exfoliative toxins remain restricted to the local site of S. aureus colonization rather than disseminating haematogenously throughout the body
Localized infection results from phage group I strains, while generalized SSSS is exclusively caused by phage group III strains
Localized bullous impetigo represents incomplete Dsg1 cleavage, whereas generalized SSSS involves complete epidermal necrosis
questions.exp:
Bullous impetigo represents the localized end of the staphylococcal exfoliative toxin disease spectrum, where exfoliative toxins produced by colonizing bacteria remain confined to the site of infection. In contrast, generalized SSSS (Ritter's disease) occurs when the focal S. aureus infection is distant and occult (nasopharynx, umbilicus, ear), allowing toxins to disseminate haematogenously throughout the body. The extent of systemic toxin dissemination, not bacterial strain virulence alone, determines the phenotype.
🏰 Palace: Picture a LOCKED BOX (localized impetigo) with toxins trapped inside the axilla versus a BURST PIÑATA (generalized SSSS) scattering exfoliative toxins everywhere through the bloodstream.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with an established diagnosis of Becker's nevus is examined. His lesion shows hyperpigmentation but minimal hypertrichosis. When the examiner firmly rubs the lesion, it becomes temporarily firmer, more elevated, and develops a characteristic 'goose-flesh' appearance. Which structure is responsible for this clinical phenomenon?
opts: Contraction of the arrector pili smooth muscles (pseudo-Darier's sign)
Temporary edema of the dermis due to mechanical trauma
Acute hyperkeratosis of the stratum corneum from friction
Capillary dilation causing transient erythema
questions.exp:
The pseudo-Darier's sign in Becker's nevus is caused by localized contraction of hypertrophied arrector pili smooth muscles in response to mechanical stimulation (rubbing), making the plaque temporarily firmer, more elevated, and 'goose-flesh' in appearance. This reflects the underlying mesodermal hamartoma affecting smooth muscle structure and function.
🏰 Palace: Rub the BECKER'S patch and watch the ARRECTOR PILI muscles ERECT like tiny soldiers standing at attention, creating GOOSE BUMPS on the archipelago—a fake DARIER'S sign (pseudo) in the boy's castle chamber.

questions.q: A 3-week-old Ashkenazi Jewish infant presents with a symmetric, erythematous, sun-sensitive rash over the cheeks in a butterfly distribution. Genetic testing reveals biallelic mutations in the BLM gene on chromosome 15q26.1. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological mechanism underlying this patient's clinical presentation?
opts: Loss of function of RecQ DNA helicase leading to defective DNA recombination and genomic instability
Pathogenic IgG autoantibodies targeting keratinocyte surface antigens in an HLA-associated manner
Transepidermal water loss due to defective tight junction proteins in the stratum corneum
Inflammatory infiltration of lymphocytes and langerhans cells triggered by unknown environmental antigens
questions.exp: Bloom syndrome is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the BLM gene encoding RecQ DNA helicase, which normally functions with topoisomerase III alpha to resolve abnormal DNA structures during replication. Loss of helicase function results in catastrophic genomic instability and increased DNA strand exchanges during mitosis. Unlike autoimmune or immunobullous disorders, Bloom syndrome involves no specific autoantigens, pathogenic antibodies, or strong HLA associations.

questions.q: A newborn is delivered at 31 weeks gestation with profoundly rigid, tightly adherent skin and severe limitation of chest wall expansion. Genetic testing reveals homozygous mutations in the ZMPSTE24 gene. Which of the following best explains the molecular pathogenesis in this case?
opts: Loss of lamin A and lamin C structural proteins due to LMNA mutations
Deficiency of zinc metallopeptidase enzyme responsible for cleaving farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A
HLA-associated autoimmune destruction of the nuclear lamina
Impaired fibroblast growth factor signaling leading to dermal hypoplasia
questions.exp: ZMPSTE24 encodes a zinc metallopeptidase essential for post-translational cleavage and processing of farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A. Without this enzyme, toxic unprocessed prelamin A accumulates at the nuclear envelope, severely distorting nuclear morphology and disrupting DNA replication and RNA transcription. This leads to catastrophic arrest of skin maturation during the second trimester.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child with Bloom syndrome presents with severe growth retardation, characteristic 'bird-like' facies, multiple café-au-lait macules, and recurrent bacterial infections. Laboratory findings reveal decreased serum IgM and IgA levels. Which of the following immunological abnormality is classically associated with this syndrome?
opts: Selective deficiency of serum IgM and IgA with normal IgG levels
Complete absence of all immunoglobulin isotypes with severe neutropenia
Elevated IgE levels with eosinophilia and elevated IL-5 production
Circulating immune complexes with C3 and C4 consumption
questions.exp: Bloom syndrome patients characteristically have deficient cellular and humoral immunity manifesting as decreased serum IgM and IgA levels. This immunological abnormality, combined with the photosensitive malar rash and growth deficiency, represents a key clinical triad distinguishing Bloom syndrome from other genodermatoses.

questions.q: Which of the following pathogenic mechanisms best explains the development of juvenile plantar dermatosis in a 6-year-old who wears plastic sneakers and frequently visits public swimming pools?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by anti-tyrosinase antibodies
Irritant contact dermatitis resulting from repeated cycling between maceration and rapid drying in an occluded, hyperhidrotic environment
Fungal infection of the stratum corneum by Trichophyton rubrum with secondary immune response
Genetic mutation in filaggrin resulting in impaired keratin cross-linking and accelerated barrier breakdown
questions.exp: Juvenile plantar dermatosis is fundamentally an irritant contact dermatitis driven by the physical transition from a highly humid, macerated environment (sweaty socks, plastic shoes, pool water) to rapid drying. This cyclic wet-dry stress is exacerbated by hyperhidrosis, synthetic occlusive footwear, and abrasive surfaces, resulting in epidermal barrier compromise. JPD is not autoimmune, not primarily fungal, and not a monogenic disorder requiring specific HLA associations or autoantibodies.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Envision a child's foot IN A PLASTIC SNEAKER (wet dungeon), then suddenly YANKED OUT into BLAZING SUN (dry)—the epidermis screams as it swells and shrinks like a tortured castle wall, irritated to tears by this brutal WET-DRY torture cycle.

questions.q: A 2-week-old neonate presents with severe generalized erythroderma, fine diffuse scaling, and profound barrier defect requiring intensive care admission. Laboratory investigations reveal hypernatremic dehydration and failure to thrive. Genetic testing subsequently confirms biallelic mutations in the SPINK5 gene. Which protein deficiency is responsible for the pathophysiology in this patient?
opts: Desmoglein 3 and desmoglein 1
LEKTI (lympho-epithelial Kazal-type related inhibitor)
Filaggrin and loricrin
Type VII collagen
questions.exp: Netherton syndrome results from SPINK5 gene mutations encoding LEKTI, a serine protease inhibitor. Loss of LEKTI function removes physiological brakes on kallikrein 5, kallikrein 7, and elastase 2, leading to premature degradation of corneodesmosomes and catastrophic skin barrier defect. This is not an autoimmune disorder and has no HLA associations, distinguishing it from immunobullous diseases.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine LEKTI as a BOUNCER holding back wild SERINE PROTEASE DANCERS in the stratum corneum castle nightclub; remove the bouncer and chaos erupts.

questions.q: A 6-month-old girl with Goltz Syndrome presents with characteristic linear atrophic skin lesions. Her dermatopathology shows profound dermal thinning with subcutaneous fat herniating upward directly adjacent to the epidermis. Which protein dysfunction directly causes this mesoectodermal defect?
opts: Impaired type IV collagen cross-linking leading to basement membrane destabilization
Loss-of-function in PORCN, which normally regulates Wnt protein membrane targeting and secretion
Aberrant keratinocyte differentiation due to filaggrin mutations
Defective elastin synthesis resulting in progressive elastic fiber fragmentation
questions.exp: Goltz Syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the PORCN gene, which encodes a crucial regulator of the Wnt signaling pathway. PORCN is responsible for membrane targeting and secretion of Wnt proteins, which are essential for normal embryonic development of mesodermal and ectodermal tissues. The absence of normal epidermal Wnt signaling causes profound failure of dermal connective tissue formation.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with symmetrical, shiny erythematous patches on the soles of his feet with superficial desquamation. The interdigital web spaces and arches of his feet are notably spared. Which histological finding would most specifically support the diagnosis of juvenile plantar dermatosis?
opts: Fungal hyphae within the stratum corneum
Inflammation specifically targeting the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts
Epidermal necrosis with hyaline deposition
Subepidermal bullae with linear IgA deposits
questions.exp: Juvenile plantar dermatosis is characterized by inflammatory changes in the epidermis, but the key distinguishing histological finding is inflammation specifically localizing to the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts. While the clinical diagnosis is primarily based on morphology and distribution, this histological focus on sweat ducts differentiates JPD from other forms of pedal dermatitis. The sparing of interdigital spaces and arches is the pathognomonic clinical clue that helps distinguish JPD from tinea pedis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a child's SWEATY SOCK getting tangled around the castle's SWEAT DUCT pipes (acrosyringium)—the inflammation clings ONLY to those ducts like wet fabric, sparing the dry arches and web spaces.

questions.q: A 6-month-old child with Netherton syndrome who initially presented with severe neonatal erythroderma is now developing migratory, polycyclic, serpiginous erythematous plaques with a distinctive double-edged scale at their margins. Which clinical phenotypic variant is this child transitioning into?
opts: Continuous skin peeling variant
Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE) variant
Ichthyosis linearis circumflexa (ILC) variant
Erythrodermic bullous variant
questions.exp: Ichthyosis linearis circumflexa (ILC) typically evolves during late infancy or early childhood as the severe neonatal erythroderma gradually subsides. The pathognomonic double-edged scale at the margins of serpiginous plaques is a distinctive hallmark of this variant. The ILC variant was historically first described by Comèl in 1949 and represents the characteristic migratory phase of Netherton syndrome.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SERPENT made of DOUBLE-EDGED SWORDS slithering through the castle—that serpentine CIRCUM-flex pattern with its DOUBLE rim is ILC's royal seal.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with painful ulcers on his tongue and buccal mucosa, followed by characteristic vesicles on his palms and soles. The vesicles are elliptical and arranged parallel to skin lines. Histology shows intraepidermal vacuolar degeneration without viral inclusion bodies. What is the most likely causative agent?
opts: Enterovirus 71
Coxsackievirus A16
Coxsackievirus A6
Herpes simplex virus type 1
questions.exp: Classic hand-foot-and-mouth disease is most commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16, presenting with a painful oropharyngeal enanthem followed by characteristic elliptical ('football-shaped') vesicles on palms and soles. The absence of viral inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells on histology specifically rules out HSV and varicella, which are present in herpetic infections.

questions.q: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of erythema toxicum neonatorum and helps distinguish it from neonatal herpes simplex or bacterial infection?
opts: Presence of vesicles exclusively on the palms and soles with systemic fever
A 'flea-bitten' appearance with central papules/pustules surrounded by irregular erythema, sparing palms and soles, and highly transient individual lesions that rarely persist >24 hours
Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with intense pain and lymphadenopathy present at birth
Pustules confined to flexural areas with maternal history of genital herpes simplex
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum classically presents with the 'flea-bitten' appearance (central papule/pustule surrounded by a sea of erythema), spares the palms and soles, and shows highly transient migratory lesions that rarely persist longer than 24 hours. These features, combined with benign systemic status, eosinophil-predominant sterile smear, and typical onset at 24–48 hours, distinguish ETN from serious infections like neonatal herpes or bacterial sepsis.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions
